completion_conditions: A finished task's lock can be released by an explicit command, and the paths become acquirable by another task.
An unfinished task's lock is refused, with the task and its status named.
The full suite, the control-plane suite, the goal-loop suite and validate_shiki stay green.

decisions: MEASURED. `.shiki/locks/` holds 69 records at `state: released` and 2 at `active`: `T-20260801T041653423255Z-2798773b` (acquired 2026-08-05 07:45, retired by the amendment in PR #300) and `T-20260805T025939375698Z-94a2fa82` (acquired 2026-08-05 03:40, task status `done`). Both tasks are finished; both still hold their declared paths.

THE ONLY RELEASE PATH, read from source: `scripts/shiki_loop.py:693-694` sets `record['state'] = 'released'` inside the loop's closeout. `grep '"released"' scripts/*.py` finds no other writer — `mergegate_check.py:1617` and `:2109` only READ the state. `scripts/shiki_cli.py:364-370` exposes exactly one lock subcommand, `acquire`. So a task that ends any way other than a loop closeout — retired, abandoned, superseded, or closed out by hand — leaks its lock permanently.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. `has_active_lock_conflict` refuses a new acquisition against an active record, and the dispatch precondition added by T-20260805T034218808409Z-0f0d9640 refuses dispatch without a grant. A leaked lock therefore blocks any FUTURE task that declares an overlapping path, and the refusal names a task that is already finished — the same three-steps-removed diagnosis that precondition exists to prevent.

RELEASE MUST BE DELIBERATE, NOT AUTOMATIC. Do not release as a side effect of a status change, a dispatch, or a validation pass: an implicit release would let an in-flight task lose its paths under it. The command is the authority for a release, exactly as `acquire` is for a grant.

FAILURE DIRECTION. Refusing a legitimate release is cheap — the operator sees a named reason and can act. Releasing a lock that is still in use is expensive: two runtimes could then hold the same paths. So the command must refuse rather than guess when the task is not finished, and every refusal must name the task and its status.

LOCK-SUFFICIENCY CHECK (2026-08-06). MUST-CHANGE: `scripts/shiki_tasks.py` (`cmd_lock_acquire` at `:982` is the sibling the new command must mirror — same record shape, same JSON result contract); `scripts/shiki_cli.py` (`:364-370` — the `lock` subparser currently has exactly one child); `tests/test_lock_release.py` (new); `scripts/test_shiki_control_plane.sh`, which owns the lock CLI end to end (`:634`, `:677`, `:698`) and is the only surface that can prove the property that matters — that after a release, a DIFFERENT task can acquire the same paths.

VERIFIED SAFE: no test greps the `lock` subparser's usage string or its `{acquire}` choice list, so adding a sibling subcommand breaks nothing. `scripts/test_shiki_goal_loop.sh:263` and `scripts/test_shiki_loop_e2e.sh:331` call `lock acquire` and are unaffected.

OUT OF SCOPE, and it must stay out: releasing the two currently-stuck records. That is a mirror edit on foreign task records, which `enforce_untrusted_shiki_mutations` rejects independently of locks. This task ships the command; using it on those two records is a separate, deliberate act.

Risk is medium: this adds a command and changes no gate, schema, workflow or approval source. Under `.shiki/guardian-policy.json` (`applies_to_risk: [high, critical]`) neither PR triggers the Guardian gate.

tasks.scope:
Add `shiki lock release <task_id>` as the deliberate counterpart to `shiki lock acquire`, and wire it into the `lock` subparser (`scripts/shiki_cli.py:364-370`, which today has exactly one child).

WHY: the ONLY release in the repository is `scripts/shiki_loop.py:693-694`, inside the loop's closeout. A task that ends any other way — retired, abandoned, superseded, or closed out by hand — holds its declared paths forever. Measured on this repository: 69 lock records are `released`, 2 are `active`, and both active ones belong to finished tasks (`T-20260801T041653423255Z-2798773b`, retired by the amendment in PR #300; `T-20260805T025939375698Z-94a2fa82`, status `done`).

It matters beyond tidiness: `has_active_lock_conflict` refuses a new acquisition against an active record, and the dispatch precondition refuses dispatch without a grant, so a leaked lock blocks any FUTURE task declaring an overlapping path — and the refusal names a task that is already finished.

SEMANTICS, stated explicitly in the docstring:
  - the command is the AUTHORITY for a release, exactly as `acquire` is for a grant. Nothing else may release a lock: not a status change, not a dispatch, not a validation pass. An implicit release could take an in-flight task's paths out from under it;
  - a lock is releasable when its task is finished. Decide finished from the task record, not from the caller's say-so, and name the rule in the docstring;
  - refuse, never guess, when the task is not finished — the reason must name the task and its status. Refusing a legitimate release is cheap (the operator reads the reason and acts); releasing a lock still in use is expensive (two runtimes could hold the same paths);
  - releasing an already-released lock is a no-op success, not an error, so the command is safe to re-run;
  - a missing or unreadable lock record is refused with the path named.

Mirror `cmd_lock_acquire` (`scripts/shiki_tasks.py:982`): same record shape, same JSON result contract, so the two read as a pair. Record who released and when, alongside the existing acquisition fields — do not delete the record.

Do NOT change the loop's own release at `scripts/shiki_loop.py:693-694`, and do NOT release the two currently-active records: that is a mirror edit on foreign task records, which `enforce_untrusted_shiki_mutations` rejects independently of locks.

TESTS. `tests/test_lock_release.py`: a finished task's lock releases and the record shows it; an unfinished task's lock is refused with the task and status named; an already-released lock re-releases as a no-op success; a missing record is refused with the path named; the release is never triggered by a status change or a dispatch. `scripts/test_shiki_control_plane.sh` owns the lock CLI end to end (`:634`, `:677`, `:698`) and must prove the property that matters and that the unit tests cannot: after a release, a DIFFERENT task declaring the SAME paths acquires them successfully.

REPRODUCIBILITY — what this task removes, and what to change to get the same result.
  Symptom: a task is finished, its lock record still reads `state: active`, and no command can change that. A later task declaring an overlapping path is refused a grant, and the refusal names the finished task.
  Measured 2026-08-06: 69 released, 2 active; both active records belong to finished tasks, acquired 2026-08-05.
  Root cause: `grep '"released"' scripts/*.py` finds exactly one writer — `shiki_loop.py:693-694` in the closeout path. `mergegate_check.py:1617` and `:2109` only read. `shiki_cli.py:364-370` exposes only `acquire`.
  Failure direction that matters: refusing a legitimate release is cheap; releasing one still in use is not. Hence refuse-not-guess, and reasons that always name the task and its status.
  Reproducible when: a finished task's lock releases, the same paths are then acquirable by a different task, and an unfinished task's lock is refused by name.
tasks.test_command: python3 -m unittest discover -s tests && bash scripts/test_shiki_control_plane.sh && bash scripts/test_shiki_goal_loop.sh && python3 scripts/validate_shiki.py --target .
